newsitem.title: THAILAND: Hopewell says Thai economy derails transit project.
newsitem.headline: Hopewell says Thai economy derails transit project.

text.p: Hopewell Holdings Ltd said on Friday it was unable to complete its long-delayed Bangkok mass transit system as planned because of adverse Thai economic conditions and the baht's recent de facto devaluation.

"The situation has changed because of the decline in the economic climate and exacerbated by the devaluation of the baht... therefore the project cannot be completed as originally planned," the firm said in a statement.
Hopewell said it wanted to complete the project and work with the Thai government to overcome financing difficulties.
Hopewell has been wrangling with successive Thai governments for a decade over the $3.2 billion elevated road and rail transit scheme which was slated to be finished by 1999.
The first phase was due to be completed by 1998 to help relieve the capital's severe trafic congestion before the Asian Games in December 1998.
The baht's 15-20 percent depreciation since its July 2 float meant international banks backing the scheme were reconsidering their commitment to the project, the statement said.
"Funding for the project in Thailand is harder. The project costs have also increased. The international banks, who are committed to the project, now need to reassess project financing," it said.
The firm also blamed a slump of the Thai property sector and proposed low fares for its failure to complete the planned project, the statement said.
Hopewell had hoped to generate project revenues by leasing commercial space under the elevated network.
The Thai property market has faced severe oversupply as the country struggles through its worst economic downturn in over a decade.
Considerable progress toward resolving the project delay had been made by Thai Transport and Communications Minister Suwat Liptapallop, the firm said.
Hopewell estimated that around 30 percent of the project's 40-km (25-mile) first phase has been completed. It said the company had spent about $560 million on the project.
The Thai government has threatened to fine Hopewell 7.5 million baht ($250,000) for each day of delay in the first phase, up to a maximum total of 134 days.
Hopewell reiterated its hope to see the project completed despite its current problems.

"Hopewell continues to be fully committed to this project ...Hopewell believes there are solutions that will enable the parties to overcome present difficulties and continues to move the project forward to completion," the firm said.
Analysts have said the Bangkok project is a drain on Wu's firm which has forced it to sell its stake in the Consolidated Power Asia (CEPA) unit to ease its cash constraints.

Anusak Intarapuvasak, deputy chairman of Hopewell (Thailand) Ltd, said the hefty baht depreciation of 15-20 percent would increase the project's original 80 billion baht investment by at least 10 billion.
He said Hopewell's prospective bank creditors would not support the project until a new feasibility study were made.
Suwat told reporters Hopewell could not raise its Thai project equity and the company's failure to secure financing had further disrupted construction of the network's concrete structures.

Senior ministry officials said due to Hopewell's problems, the government would study the implications for the project if it decided to exercise its right of abrogating the concession awarded to the company.
(US$1 = 30 baht)
